meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Now We’re Just Haggling Over the Price'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bertrand Russell. It is an anonymous joke: the 1936 first printing tells it of Lord Beaverbrook, and the famous names were swapped in later.

answer.label: Not Bertrand Russell — an anonymous joke
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented telling: New York Post, 6 June 1936 · told of Lord Beaverbrook
answer.sourceLine: No source ties this line to Bertrand Russell. Quote Investigator ↗ lists Russell as one of the famous men the role has been assigned to — alongside Churchill, Shaw, Groucho Marx, Mark Twain, W. C. Fields, H. G. Wells and Woodrow Wilson — and finds that the earliest example of the story it has located, a June 1936 column in the “New York Post”, features none of them. It tells the joke of the press baron Lord Beaverbrook, and its punch line is not “haggling over the price” at all.

source.heading: The earliest documented telling

docMeta.dd: “Lyons Den” by Leonard Lyons, New York Post
Lord Beaverbrook (Max Aitken) — not Bertrand Russell
“Now we’re trying to determine the degree” — not “haggling over the price”

source.excerpt: They’re telling this of Lord Beaverbrook and a visiting Yankee actress. In a game of hypothetical questions, Beaverbrook asked the lady: “Would you live with a stranger if he paid you £1,000,000?” She answered “Yes.” “And if he paid you £5?” The irate lady fumed: “£5? What do you think I am?” Beaverbrook replied: “We’ve already established that. Now we’re trying to determine the degree.”
trail: 1936. Newspaper columnist Leonard Lyons prints the story in the New York Post, told of Lord Beaverbrook. This is the earliest example Quote Investigator ↗ has located, and it names none of the men the joke is credited to today. Two weeks later, on 19 June, the Evening Review of Niagara Falls, Ontario, reprints Lyons with an acknowledgement — the joke has crossed the border before any famous name is attached.

1937. It goes national: syndicated columnist O. O. McIntyre carries the story on 2 January 1937, a citation documented in the American Dialect Society research thread ↗ that preceded the QI article, and the University of Michigan humour magazine Gargoyle runs a matching version that April, dated by Quote Investigator ↗.

1955–1962. In QI’s chronology the “haggling” wording first appears in a US House subcommittee hearing of 12 October 1955, used as an allusion to a story the room already knows; by January 1962 a newspaper letter credits it to Churchill ↗.

Today. Wikiquote carries an un-named version of the joke in the Misattributed section of its Shaw ↗ page, sourced to the 1936 Beaverbrook telling, though the Shaw-named dialogue still sits under Disputed; on the Churchill ↗ page it survives only as an unsourced Talk-page anecdote, where a 2020 request to move it to the article’s Misattributed box is still unactioned. Churchill historian Richard Langworth calls the Churchill telling “Pure nonsense” ↗. No comparable defence has ever been mounted for the Russell version, because no source exists to defend.
source.excerptNote: The 1936 column as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. Note the euphemism: the column says “live with” rather than “sleep with”, in keeping with what a 1936 newspaper would print. And note that the telling is already second-hand — “They’re telling this of Lord Beaverbrook.”
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted here. The punch line is an anonymous joke with no identified author, so there is no work whose first publication date would settle it. The earliest documented printing is a 1936 newspaper column by Leonard Lyons, and whether that column’s US copyright was renewed — the question that decides the status of American works published in 1936 — has not been established here.

author.name: Max Aitken, Lord Beaverbrook
author.heading: The man the joke was first told about
author.bio: William Maxwell Aitken, 1st Baron Beaverbrook (25 May 1879 – 9 June 1964) was a Canadian-born press baron who owned the Daily Express and the Evening Standard and served in British government as Minister of Aircraft Production and Lord Privy Seal. He is the earliest famous name known to be attached to this joke — but attached is all it is. The 1936 column that first prints it opens “They’re telling this of Lord Beaverbrook,” which is a columnist repeating gossip, not a witness recording a remark. Beaverbrook has no better claim to the line than Russell does; he was simply first in a queue of interchangeable famous men.

misattribution.heading: A joke with a revolving cast
misattribution.intro: This is not a quotation with one wrong owner — it is a joke that has been fitted to whichever famous man a teller finds convenient. Quote Investigator ↗ names eight of them, and finds an early telling that uses none.

items.why: Russell is one of the eight famous men Quote Investigator ↗ lists as having been assigned the role. Its chronology — running from 1936 to 1985 — contains no telling that features Russell, and no letter, book, lecture or interview of his has been produced for it.

A letter in the Nevada State Journal of 20 January 1962 credits the punch line to Churchill, one of the earliest namings QI records. Churchill historian Richard Langworth calls the story “Pure nonsense” ↗ with no attribution to Churchill. Wikiquote’s Churchill talk page ↗ goes less far: it files the exchange among unsourced anecdotes, calling it “a very old joke” and “very unlikely though not impossible” as a Churchill original, and the article itself carries no entry for it either way.

John Allen Paulos still credited Shaw in 1985 while admitting the joke “seems more appropriate with Groucho.” In July 2013 Wikiquote editors ↗ cited QI and added the anecdote to Shaw’s Misattributed section — though the Shaw-named dialogue still sits under Disputed on the article today.

items.who: Groucho Marx, Mark Twain, W. C. Fields, H. G. Wells, Woodrow Wilson
items.why: Gershon Legman’s Rationale of the Dirty Joke (1968) already described it as a story told of almost every modern celebrity beginning with President Wilson and H. G. Wells ↗ — which is the clearest sign that the famous name is decoration, not evidence.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest example Quote Investigator ↗ has located is a 6 June 1936 “Lyons Den” column in the New York Post, told of Lord Beaverbrook and an unnamed actress — and even there the punch line is “Now we’re trying to determine the degree.” The “haggling over the price” wording, and every famous name now attached to it, came later.

context.heading: Why every clever man gets credited with it
lead: The joke has one structural requirement: the man delivering the punch line must be famous enough for cruelty to read as wit. That is why the cast keeps rotating. Bertrand Russell, Winston Churchill, George Bernard Shaw, Groucho Marx, Mark Twain, W. C. Fields, H. G. Wells and Woodrow Wilson have all been dropped into the role, and the woman — the actual target of the line — almost never gets a name at all.

The wording drifted as much as the cast did. The 1936 telling ends “Now we’re trying to determine the degree,” which is stiffer and less quotable than what replaced it. In Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ the “haggling” phrasing does not surface until a US House subcommittee hearing of 12 October 1955, where a congressman uses it as shorthand for a story he assumes everyone already knows. By then it needed no set-up, and no author.
detailsBody: 6 June 1936 — Leonard Lyons prints it in the “Lyons Den” column of the New York Post, told of Lord Beaverbrook and “a visiting Yankee actress.” This is the earliest example Quote Investigator ↗ has found.

1937 — It spreads: a Niagara Falls paper reprints Lyons in June 1936, syndicated columnist O. O. McIntyre reprints it on 2 January 1937, and the University of Michigan humour magazine Gargoyle runs a close match that April.
1944–1946 — Coronet, Reader’s Digest, the trade journal Excavating Engineer and the lawyers’ magazine Case and Comment all carry versions; the anonymous-lawyer variant moves the scene to a courtroom.

1955–1962 — The punch line detaches from the story. A congressman alludes to it in a 1955 hearing; sociologist Peter L. Berger prints a full “haggling over the price” version in The Precarious Vision (1961); and a January 1962 letter in the Nevada State Journal credits it to Winston Churchill.

1965–1985 — Arthur Herzog calls it an “old joke”; Gershon Legman’s Rationale of the Dirty Joke (1968) says it has been told of almost every modern celebrity beginning with Wilson and H. G. Wells; and John Allen Paulos, printing it in 1985, openly swaps Shaw out for Groucho because it suits Groucho better.
context.pull: The famous name is the interchangeable part. The joke is the fixed one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located example is a June 1936 'Lyons Den' column by Leonard Lyons in the New York Post telling the joke of Lord Beaverbrook, with the punch line 'We've already established that. Now we're trying to determine the degree.'; QI lists Bertrand Russell among the men assigned the role; QI concludes the anecdote began as a fictional joke with famous men substituted in. Chronology includes the 19 June 1936 reprint in the Evening Review of Niagara Falls, Ontario (acknowledging Lyons), the 2 January 1937 O. O. McIntyre syndicated column in the Muscatine Journal and News-Tribune, the April 1937 University of Michigan Gargoyle version, 1944 Coronet, 1945 Excavating Engineer and Reader's Digest, 1946 Case and Comment, the 12 October 1955 House subcommittee hearing using 'haggling about the price', Peter L. Berger's 1961 The Precarious Vision, the 20 January 1962 Nevada State Journal letter crediting Churchill, Arthur Herzog's 1965 'old joke', Legman's 1968 Rationale of the Dirty Joke, and Paulos's 1985 I Think, Therefore I Laugh.

Wikiquote's Churchill talk page carries the anecdote under '== Unsourced == / === Anecdotal dialogue ===' with the parenthetical 'This is a very old joke where the participants vary dramatically from each telling. It's very unlikely though not impossible that the joke originated from Churchill.' User:Mcljlm asked on 7 May 2020 that it be moved to the article's Misattributed box; the request drew no reply, and the live Churchill article contains no matching entry (raw wikitext grepped for 'haggl', 'established what', 'five pounds', '£5' — zero matches).

Wikiquote's George Bernard Shaw talk page discusses the anecdote, notes it has been credited to Churchill (most often), Mark Twain, Bertrand Russell and W. C. Fields as well as Shaw, and records Llarq citing Quote Investigator on 8 July 2013 ('highly unlikely that the quote originated with Shaw') with Spannerjam replying on 10 July 2013, 'I added it to the misattributed section of the page.' On the live Shaw article the un-named form sits under '== Misattributed ==' sourced to the 1936 Beaverbrook telling, while the Shaw-named dialogue remains under '== Disputed =='.

Richard M. Langworth, Senior Fellow of the Hillsdale College Churchill Project, addresses the 'sleep with me for five pounds / haggling over the price' story and calls it 'Pure nonsense', stating there is no attribution to Churchill and that it is out of character.

The December 2011 American Dialect Society (ADS-L) thread documents early citations of the anecdote, including the 2 January 1937 O. O. McIntyre syndicated column crediting Lyons and featuring Lord Beaverbrook, the University of Michigan Gargoyle version, 1944 Coronet, 1945 Excavating Engineer and Reader's Digest, and the 1965 Herzog 'haggling' wording, and notes the earliest evidence features Beaverbrook rather than the celebrities usually credited.

William Maxwell Aitken, 1st Baron Beaverbrook (25 May 1879 - 9 June 1964) was a Canadian-British newspaper publisher and politician, proprietor of the Daily Express and Evening Standard, who served as Minister of Aircraft Production (1940-1941) and Lord Privy Seal (1943-1945).
